Guides

What to introduce, and when

There is no set calendar for which vegetable comes when. There is a good reason to bring in allergens early and keep them in the diet.

Findings

‘One new food at a time’ is a habit, not a rule. New allergens are easier to judge if they come one at a time. Everyday vegetables don’t need a three-day wait.
Gluten can come in with the first foods. Delaying it doesn’t prevent coeliac disease. Do avoid very large amounts in the first weeks.
Before one, cow’s milk isn’t the main drink. Small amounts in a sauce, in porridge, or as yogurt are fine from the start of solids.

Skip the long ladder

Older weaning charts added one new vegetable every few days and held back meat, wheat, egg, and fish until late in the first year. That made for tidy feeding diaries and poor iron intake. It also missed the window when introducing allergens early seems to protect.

Introduce one new common allergen on a morning when your baby is well: give a small amount and watch. You can repeat it the next day. Other new foods, like a different vegetable, can share the plate. If there’s no reaction, keep that allergen in the diet several times a week. One taste isn’t enough to maintain tolerance.

Gluten, egg, fish, and the rest

ESPGHAN says gluten can be introduced between 4 and 12 months, avoiding large amounts in the first weeks and throughout infancy. A portion of pasta or bread is fine. A pile of biscuits isn’t.

Cook egg all the way through. Fish should be boneless and fully cooked. Peanut and other nuts should be smooth butter, thinned into food: never whole, and never a thick spoonful. Sesame means tahini, not a sprinkle of whole seeds. You’ll find the details, and the plan for high-risk babies and peanut, on the allergen page.

Milk as a drink and milk as a food

Breast milk or infant formula stays the main drink until 12 months. Using whole cow’s milk as that drink raises the risk of low iron intake, and it’s no substitute for formula. After the first birthday, whole cow’s milk can become the main drink, at roughly 350 to 400 ml a day so it doesn’t crowd out meals.

Yogurt, small amounts of pasteurised cheese, and milk cooked into a sauce count as food, not drinks, and are fine from six months. Unpasteurised milk and mould-ripened or blue cheeses stay off the menu for the first few years.
